#71009. Mauricio Pochettino’s USMNT time will be remembered fondly, but it wasn’t transformational

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1018 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theguardian ↗ Open Full Page

Mauricio Pochettino’s USMNT time will be remembered fondly, but it wasn’t transformational

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1018 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The incoming Manchester United manager improved the US team’s culture and competitiveness, but could not bring about sea change in two years.
  • In a theater high up in a midtown Manhattan skyscraper built from lots of glass, a highlight reel played to deafening music.
  • In a recent development, pochettino held court for three-quarters of an hour in his signature blend of Spanglish before the assembled media and a grab bag of sponsors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The incoming Manchester United manager improved the US team’s culture and competitiveness, but could not bring about sea change in two years.

In a theater high up in a midtown Manhattan skyscraper built from lots of glass, a highlight reel played to deafening music. And then, on “a monumental day for US Soccer”, federation president, Cindy Parlow Cone, confirmed they had bagged their man, Mauricio Pochettino, to become the highest-profile United States manager in the men’s national team’s history.

In a recent development, pochettino held court for three-quarters of an hour in his signature blend of Spanglish before the assembled media and a grab bag of sponsors. Then he recorded some TV hits. And after that, in a bit of accidental prescience, he went off to record a podcast with Gary Neville.

Two years, two months, and a week later, he presided over the USMNT’s untroubled 2-0 win over Haiti in Cincinnati on Tuesday, putting a bow on an 8-0 aggregate victory in the Concacaf Nations League quarter-finals. He did a lot of hugging afterwards, a staple of what was briefly mooted as Pochismo. He posed for a group picture with federation staffers. There were tears in the locker room.

In a recent development, after a 6-0 romp in the first leg on Saturday, Pochettino left his starting XI unchanged, raising some eyebrows. Perhaps he hoped to leave with another emphatic result; maybe he was buffing up his final stats in charge of the USA; or possibly he was legitimately concerned about giving away a lead of half a dozen goals.

It will probably be the last time in quite a long while that Pochettino enjoys a pair of consecutive lopsided victories. He boarded a private jet after the game to take over Manchester United just as soon it landed in England in the morning, leaving a situation where he enjoyed a bank vault’s worth of credit for one where his every result will be dissected and scrutinized for his viability in the job.

Recent findings suggest that for all the hype, for the $6m annual salary – about double what the previous record earner at the federation, Jürgen Klinsmann, had made – and for all the talk of belief and culture and fight, what did Pochettino actually leave behind for his successor to build on? He was impactful, certainly, turning around a moody and slumping generation ambling into a home World Cup bereft of momentum or much discernible enthusiasm. The Argentinian roused the ballyhooed golden generation for four-fifths of a very strong World Cup, turning in displays more convincing and dominant than the program has ever managed on that stage – until it all came undone against Belgium in the last 16.

Industry observers note that his time in charge was notable, absolutely. Pochettino got, and brought, lots of attention to the team, although it’s hard to say whether a more workaday manager might not have ridden that same World Cup wave, as the voice of the co-hosts.

Industry observers note that pochettino wasn’t the first USMNT manager to try to play more expansively, more technically, in a more aesthetically pleasing way. Klinsmann tried it, and Gregg Berhalter tried it, too. But Klinsmann didn’t have the players, and Berhalter’s weren’t ready for it. Pochettino did and they were, at long last, and he introduced a tactical sophistication, with deft attacking patterns that regularly unlocked useful spaces.

He also wasn’t the first USMNT manager to fixate on culture and give young talent a chance. But through his selections and his messaging, he reinstated an internal competition for playing time that had seeped away under several consecutive and at times complacent administrations. And he deepened the player pool considerably. Perhaps any old head coach would have spotted the glut of gifted teenagers pushing through and had the wherewithal to bring them along, but Pochettino deserves credit for leaning on the young players, handing them meaningful minutes and responsibility.

While Pochettino leaves the USMNT better than he found them, his spell in charge was not transformational. He brought the Americans no further at a World Cup than they had been before. His statistics – victories in 62% of his matches; 2.08 goals scored per game; 1.29 conceded – are more or less in line with the numbers put up by his permanent predecessors. He did not win the Concacaf Gold Cup or the Nations League when he was occasioned to.

Nor did he take the US to their first World Cup in four decades, as Bob Gansler did in 1990. Or make them respectable on that stage, as Bora Milutinovic did in 1994. Or bring about their breakthrough, as Bruce Arena did in 2002. Or rebuild the program from its modern nadir, as Berhalter did in his first tenure. It is a sign of growth, perhaps, that the strides available to be made were smaller. You can only overcome the challenges you are faced with, after all.

Whatever the case, Pochettino will be remembered fondly by most. He smiled and joked a lot and did his best to say interesting things. He could be spiky, from time to time, but mostly injected an environment that had grown stale and dour with joy.

According to recent reports, pochettino, by all accounts, had a good time stateside, commuting here from his homes in London and Barcelona. He enjoyed watching NFL games and attended the Cincinnati Bengals’ home victory over the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday. He got into country music, apparently. “Only we can say thank you,” Pochettino said in his final news conference, on behalf of his staff. “Thank you so much, and always we are going to keep the good memories.”.

In a recent development, the USMNT, too, largely enjoyed their time with their famous coach. They made some nice memories together. But he may not have been here long enough to fundamentally change their trajectory.

Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: US Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts, which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.

Klopp wants Infantino out as FIFA candidate deadline looms

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (867 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Germany coach Jürgen Klopp has become the latest prominent football figure to call for change at the top of FIFA.
  • "Regarding Gianni Infantino, surely the next person to come along can do a better job," he mentioned on Sunday.
  • But with time running out before the November 18 deadline for new candidates for the presidency of world football's governing body, Infantino is looking overwhelmingly likely to win another term.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Germany coach Jürgen Klopp has become the latest prominent football figure to call for change at the top of FIFA.

"Regarding Gianni Infantino, surely the next person to come along can do a better job," he mentioned on Sunday.

But with time running out before the November 18 deadline for new candidates for the presidency of world football's governing body, Infantino is looking overwhelmingly likely to win another term.

"There are people who truly care about the future of football, people who aren't driven by financial interests," Klopp noted ahead of Germany's Nations League match against the Netherlands on Monday.

"If someone like that were to step up — if someone like that were to become president — I think that would be a significant improvement.".

If that person is waiting in the wings, they're leaving it late to step on the stage. Despite a raft of federations and continental confederations, including Germany, UEFA (Europe), CONCACAF (North and Central America and the Caribbean) and AFC (Asia), calling for Infantino's head in the wake of his plan to sell off part of the World Cup earlier this year, the incumbent appears to have stopped the bleeding.

That initiative, which involved forming a subsidiary arm of FIFA called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) in order to sell off part of its commercial operations to investors including Joshua Kushner — brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner — was widely panned before being abandoned.

It followed on from widespread criticism of Infantino's awarding of a newly introduced FIFA Peace Prize to Trump, the overturning of a red card for US national team player Folarin Balogun, and with Trump's involvement, at the World Cup and a host of other controversies.

Since then, though, many public critics have backtracked amid FIFA promising to release an extra $2.7bn (€2.45bn) from its reserves over the next four years to the federations, increasing their total investment to $6.35bn.

Perhaps the most significant of these u-turns came from the AFC, who went from saying Infantino had committed a "fundamental breach of trust" in August, to offering the Swiss its "full commitment to supporting you and your leadership as you seek a upcoming mandate as the FIFA president" in October.

According to recent reports, those words were spoken by AFC President, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, who ran against Infantino when he first won the top job at FIFA in 2016. He will not run again and stated that "my feeling is, I'm sure, the feeling of most of my members," in regard to Infantino.

Sources indicate that proof that the sentiment is not universal comes in the shape of Kozo Tashima, the honorary president of the Japan Football Association (JFA). Tashima is one of only two people to confirm they will oppose Infantino in the March 2027 presidential elections.

The 68-year-old is a well respected figure in Asian football politics and will have no problem meeting the threshold of support from five of FIFA's 211 federations. This is not like the other candidate, former Swiss international player Ramon Vega, who is an enormous outsider. Tashima appears to be running on the basis that he will be able to chart a calmer path at FIFA.

Sources indicate that "I am grateful that I can make this announcement with the full support of the Japan Football Association," Tashima told the Japanese newspaper Sports Nippon. "It's not about winning or losing but about conveying to the world the honest, sound and upright attitude that Japanese football has built. What FIFA needs now are these values that we have protected. I have decided to run in order to make this appeal to the world.".

According to recent reports, but the numbers are against him. Though support from within the confederations may not be total, the backing of AFC and the African confederation (CAF) is a huge boost for Infantino, with those two alone making up 101 votes, almost enough for a majority.

Industry observers note that in fact, the only real concern remaining for Infantino remains UEFA. The European federation, headed by Aleksander Ceferin, is a major revenue source for FIFA but the two organizations are at loggerheads. As well as a war of words, UEFA are seeking to obtain evidence for a potential Swiss criminal case against Infantino in regards to FFE. FIFA have called this a "smear campaign" and a "fishing expedition".

It has been revealed that but, so far, UEFA has not put up a candidate. Former Arsenal coach turned FIFA Chief of Global Football Development, Arsene Wenger was thought to be a contender but has now ruled himself out. Wenger's compatriot, Philippe Diallo, has since emerged as another option, with The Guardian reporting on Monday that the French Football Federation president could be announced on Tuesday.

While Europe is football's powerbase, particularly from a club perspective, UEFA will need Diallo, or any candidate they can convince to run, to win votes from outside its 55 nations to have any chance of success, particularly with Tashima likely to split any challenge. Even if a candidate appears before the November 18 deadline, Klopp's hope for change appears to be a long shot.

It has been revealed that those offences all came between 2009 and 2018. City have denied any wrongdoing and appealed against all of the charges against them.

The club's longest-serving first-team player who was purchased from another club is Portuguese centre-back and club captain Ruben Dias, who joined from Benfica in 2020.

Norway striker Erling Haaland is the next longest-serving arrival, joining from Borussia Dortmund in the summer of 2022.

Midfielder Phil Foden is the only player to have played for the club during the period in which they breached the league's financial rules, but was not a senior signing having come through the club's youth ranks.

Foden, 26, made his first-team debut in a Champions League match against Feyenoord in November 2017.

Like Foden, versatile midfielder Rico Lewis is also a product of the club's academy but did not make his senior debut until August 2022.

All of the club's other senior players were signed between 2023 and 2026.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Arsenal forward Kai Havertz is among the players to have received two yellow cards in this season's Champions League.
  • Players will receive a one-match ban should they receive four yellow cards before the semi-finals of the Champions League.
  • This rule runs from the start of the league phase until the end of the quarter-finals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arsenal forward Kai Havertz is among the players to have received two yellow cards in this season's Champions League.

Players will receive a one-match ban should they receive four yellow cards before the semi-finals of the Champions League.

This rule runs from the start of the league phase until the end of the quarter-finals. After then, all yellow cards are wiped out and players cannot be suspended for multiple yellow cards.

Yellow cards that result in a red card during a match do not count towards a player's tally, as a separate suspension will be served.

The same rules apply for both the Europa League and the Conference League.

During the opening three rounds of the Champions League, 16 players received two yellow cards, meaning they are now two cautions away from a one-match ban.

Shakhtar Donetsk's Marlon Gomes, Villarreal's Santiago Mourino and Inter Milan's Hakan Calhanoglu are each on three yellow cards, putting them on the brink of a ban.

Players can also be suspended if they pick up six, eight or 10 yellow cards. This would also result in a one-match suspension every time a player hits an even number of yellow cards above four.

Red cards result in a one-match suspension, with Bayern Munich's Michael Olise missing his side's earlier clash with Arsenal after being sent off against Viking in the previous round of fixtures.

Uefa may increase the length of a red card ban for serious offences such as violent conduct.

Marlon Gomes (Shakhtar Donetsk).

Josko Gvardiol (Manchester City).

Matheus Cunha* (Manchester United).

Alessandro Bastoni* (Inter Milan).

Cristian Martinez (Slovan Bratislava).

Alexis Mac Allister (Liverpool).

*denotes two yellows that resulted in a red card.

Blackburn rally without Tony Mowbray to deny Burnley long-awaited home win

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Todd Cantwell’s penalty earned Blackburn a 2-2 draw at Burnley in their first match since head coach Tony Mowbray stepped back because of health issues.
  • In a gripping, physical East Lancashire derby, the home side led twice, through Largie Ramazani’s rising first-half drive and Jaydon Banel’s steered finish after the break.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Todd Cantwell’s penalty earned Blackburn a 2-2 draw at Burnley in their first match since head coach Tony Mowbray stepped back because of health issues.

In a gripping, physical East Lancashire derby, the home side led twice, through Largie Ramazani’s rising first-half drive and Jaydon Banel’s steered finish after the break.

But Andri Gudjohnsen scored Blackburn’s first equaliser, then earned the penalty which Cantwell converted.

Burnley remain deep in relegation trouble, without a home league victory for 400 days, having once again failed to hold on to a lead. They have now dropped 25 points from winning positions in the Championship this season.

Blackburn wanted a victory not just for local pride, but to honour Mowbray, who turned 63 on Sunday, and for whom this was set to be a 900th match in management before his announcement on Tuesday that he would be stepping back.

Their players warmed up in T-shirts bearing the message ‘We’re with you, Tony’ on the back and the number 900 on the front.

Coaches Damien Johnson and Mike Dodds have taken charge in Mowbray’s absence and had to reshuffle the defence when Tom Atcheson was concussed after receiving a boot to the face in the third minute.

Stand-in goalkeeper Aynsley Pears, playing after Balazs Toth suffered a broken hand on international duty with Hungary, pushed over a fierce deflected shot from Banel, but was at fault when Ramazani gave Burnley a 27th-minute lead.

The on-loan Leeds winger cut in from the right and fired a shot that flew into the roof of the net right by Pears, who was too slow to react.

It has been revealed that but Gudjohnsen equalised four minutes later, racing on to a Harry Pickering long ball that drifted over Burnley centre-back Max Alleyne, and steering a sweet shot beyond goalkeeper Max Weiss for his 12th goal of the season. The Icelander celebrated by grabbing a T-shirt paying tribute to Mowbray from a photographer and displaying it for the cameras.

Blackburn finished the first half strongly, with Cantwell firing over a good chance, before Banel restored Burnley’s lead six minutes into the second half, running unchallenged to place a shot into the far corner as defender Hayden Carter backed off.

The home side were fortunate to escape a strong penalty appeal just before the hour mark as Cantwell burst into the penalty area and saw two attempted crosses both strike the arm of Igor Julio.

Blackburn did get a penalty with 16 minutes left as Josh Laurent, attempting to clear a low cross, failed to spot Gudjohnsen darting in from behind him and caught the striker’s leg. Cantwell drove the penalty straight down the middle to make it 2-2.

Gudjohnsen thought he had given Blackburn the lead two minutes later, when he controlled and drove a low shot against the base of the post with Weiss a spectator, but neither side could find a winner.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s fair to say that anyone would be spoilt for choice when it comes to selecting the most physical challenge of Graeme Souness’ career.
  • The fiery Scot was one of the most uncompromising players of his - or anyone else’s - generation, with the former Liverpool skipper taking no prisoners as he patrolled the middle of the park.
  • But even by his standards, one challenge stands out above all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s fair to say that anyone would be spoilt for choice when it comes to selecting the most physical challenge of Graeme Souness’ career.

The fiery Scot was one of the most uncompromising players of his - or anyone else’s - generation, with the former Liverpool skipper taking no prisoners as he patrolled the middle of the park.

But even by his standards, one challenge stands out above all. That came in a European Cup tie against Steaua Bucharest in 1987, when Liverpool welcomed the Romanian side back to Anfield.

“We'd gone out there and lost the first leg 2-0,” Souness recalls to FourFourTwo. “There was a guy called Marius Lacatus who was going around topping people.

“In the second game, I thought, ‘If I get half a chance, I'll give him one.’”.

It didn’t take long for that chance to present itself.

“After about 10 minutes, I went through this guy at groin height – when he went down and rolled over, I thought, ‘I've got the wrong player…' Lacatus was 15 or 20 yards away, laughing at me because he thought I was getting sent off.”.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Much to Souness’ surprise, that red card didn’t come.

Sources indicate that “When I made the challenge, I thought, ‘F**k, I've got a problem here', so I went down as well, pretending someone had kicked me. It worked! I should have been arrested and spent time behind bars…”.

The Scot would recieve his fair share of red and yellow cards during his illustrious playing career, but as he looks back on his career, he does not regret this approach.

Sources indicate that “The reality is that I was sent off six or seven times in my career,” he continues. “Not bad given the nature of the game in those days. Every team had a couple of people who would get involved in the physical aspect.

“At Liverpool, people didn't say, ‘Oh we're playing Liverpool today, let's have a jolly nice game of football.' It was, ‘Let's put a few of them on their backsides and see how they deal with it.' If you stood up to that and it settled into a game of football, generally we'd win.

“We could do both – we had to.”.

In addition to his journalist work, Mewis is also the author of four football history books that include times on Leeds United and the England national team. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

Which game will Chelsea's Palmer miss after red card?

📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (276 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Co

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cole Palmer was sent off in the second half of Chelsea's 2-0 loss at Stamford Bridge.
  • Chelsea's Cole Palmer will not miss the Blues' Premier League meeting with Manchester United on Saturday, despite being sent off in his side's last Premier League match.
  • Palmer was shown two yellow cards in the second half of the Blues' defeat by rivals Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cole Palmer was sent off in the second half of Chelsea's 2-0 loss at Stamford Bridge.

Chelsea's Cole Palmer will not miss the Blues' Premier League meeting with Manchester United on Saturday, despite being sent off in his side's last Premier League match.

Palmer was shown two yellow cards in the second half of the Blues' defeat by rivals Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday. That dismissal meant that Palmer was handed a one-match ban.

Recent findings suggest that the England playmaker was shown his first caution for an off-the-ball incident involving Spurs' Mateus Fernandes. He was then shown a second yellow card for a foul on Conor Gallagher.

In most cases, this would be served in that team's next Premier League match. However, Palmer will not miss Chelsea's meeting with United at Stamford Bridge.

Instead, Palmer will be banned for the Blues' EFL Cup fourth-round match away at Liverpool on Wednesday night.

This is because red card suspensions are carried out across domestic competitions rather than being specific to the competition they were received in.

Suspensions for an accumulation of yellow cards across a campaign are served in the competition in which they are received.

So while the Blues will miss Palmer for their trip to Anfield, he will be available to face United three days after the club's cup tie on Merseyside.

#70999. Latest Update: How to turn impostor syndrome into a superpower

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1747 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nature ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: How to turn impostor syndrome into a superpower

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1747 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, impostor syndrome — a fear of being less competent than people think — is common in researchers.
  • In 2021, Kwabena Boahen Asare found himself in at the deep end when he joined a skin cancer laboratory to gain hands-on research experience.
  • For Asare, who was a first-year undergraduate student at Dartmouth College in Hanover, New Hampshire, at the time, it was an exciting but daunting prospect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, impostor syndrome — a fear of being less competent than people think — is common in researchers. Credit: Gandee Vasan/Getty.

In 2021, Kwabena Boahen Asare found himself in at the deep end when he joined a skin cancer laboratory to gain hands-on research experience.

For Asare, who was a first-year undergraduate student at Dartmouth College in Hanover, New Hampshire, at the time, it was an exciting but daunting prospect. Not only was he the sole bachelor’s programme student working alongside senior researchers with years of experience under their belts, he was also the only Black person in the lab. Although Asare’s mentor and colleagues were supportive and encouraging, he felt overwhelmed and out of his depth. “There was a steep learning curve,” he indicates.

Industry observers note that at the time, Asare viewed his struggles as a sign that he didn’t belong in research. This feeling was compounded by the fact that he was surrounded by colleagues who didn’t share his background as a first-generation student from Ghana.

In a recent development, his experience, and those of many like him, is commonly labelled as impostor syndrome — the fear of not being as competent or knowledgeable as other people think, despite objective accomplishments. In a world that often prizes unflinching self-confidence and boldness, impostor syndrome is usually cast as a psychological flaw that the individual needs to ‘fix’. But it can be a natural response to working in a challenging environment or striving towards an ambitious goal, organizational psychologists say.

Sources indicate that impostor syndrome can also be a reaction to systemic bias and exclusion in the workplace, particularly for people from under-represented groups, including women, claims Ruchika Malhotra, an inclusion strategist and founder of Candour, a workplace consultancy in Seattle, Washington. The company advises organizations on strategies to create diverse teams and inclusive cultures. One study1 conducted at universities in the United States found that women who work in scientific fields that particularly value intellectual brilliance are more likely to feel like impostors than are their male colleagues.

How I tackled post-PhD impostor syndrome.

How I tackled post-PhD impostor syndrome.

In a recent development, much of the discussion about impostor syndrome pathologizes healthy self-doubt and shifts the responsibility onto individuals instead of the environments that exclude and marginalize them in the first place, adds Malhotra. “A lot of the ways that it’s been talked about haven’t been constructive,” she notes.

It has been revealed that although it comes with drawbacks, in some situations, impostor syndrome can be beneficial. For instance, it can help people be better prepared and more focused, particularly when they have a long to-do list.

“Impostor thoughts are almost like your superpower when things get pretty overwhelming,” states Basima Tewfik, an organizational psychologist who studies impostor syndrome at Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge.

Looking back, Asare states that his impostor syndrome prompted him to reflect on why he wanted to become a researcher in the first place. It has also made him more conscious of his resilience, how he needs to improve and when to seek help, as well as giving him more empathy. This has made him better able to support younger students and researchers who are feeling out of place. “It became my strength,” says Asare, who is now an oncology researcher and consultant at Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center in Lebanon, Upcoming Hampshire.

Recent findings suggest that impostor syndrome was first described as ‘impostor phenomenon’ in a 1978 paper on high-achieving women2 co-authored by psychologists Pauline Clance and Suzanne Imes, both then at Georgia State University in Atlanta. They wrote that people who experience this phenomenon “maintain a strong belief that they are not intelligent; in fact they are convinced that they have fooled anyone who thinks otherwise”.

In the decades since, impostor phenomenon has morphed into a syndrome, even though it isn’t a medical diagnosis, nor is it classified as a psychiatric disorder. A review published in 20233 suggests that around 70% of people will feel unworthy of their accomplishments at some point in their lives. These feelings are even more prevalent in academia, with a 2012 study4 finding that as many as 82% of graduate students experience impostor syndrome to at least some degree. This pattern of thinking often affects high achievers and is associated with lower job satisfaction, hindered performance and burnout. Although some studies, including the 2012 paper, suggest that impostor syndrome affects mostly women and people from other groups under-represented in academia, others argue that it arises in specific situations rather than among particular groups. Relatively few studies have investigated whether commonly cited strategies, such as listing one’s accomplishments and accepting compliments from others, are actually effective.

Impostor syndrome has become a catchphrase in popular culture, with dozens of articles, books and courses describing what it is and how people can overcome it. But in the scientific literature, at least, the exact definition of impostor syndrome, or phenomenon, varies widely. This has created a murky picture of what it really is and how it affects people, states Tewfik. “There are a lot of different ways people describe this phenomenon,” she says. The loose definition has made it easy to confuse impostor syndrome, which causes people to make inferences about what other people think of them, with regular self-doubt, which is more of a personal reflection of your own capabilities, according to Tewfik.

‘Maybe I was never meant to be in science’: how impostor syndrome seizes scientist mothers.

‘Maybe I was never meant to be in science’: how impostor syndrome seizes scientist mothers.

It has been revealed that much of the research on impostor syndrome has also used measures that have made it difficult to distinguish from other psychological patterns, such as negative affectivity, a personality trait that is linked to a tendency to experience negative emotions such as fear, anxiety and insecurity, adds Tewfik. This crossover might explain why most studies on impostor syndrome have shown only negative outcomes, such as a lack of career planning and low motivation to lead5. “It’s possible that what we’ve been studying is actually something much more akin to fear,” claims Tewfik.

This overly negative slant is exacerbated by the fact that many workplaces, including academic ones, place too much emphasis on self-confidence, says Tomas Chamorro-Premuzic, an organizational psychologist at University College London. One 2024 study6 found that workers who display confidence are perceived as more competent and dominant, irrespective of their actual ability.

Industry observers note that if impostor syndrome hinders a person’s ability to work or form relationships, it’s usually a symptom of a deeper problem or clinical condition, such as an anxiety disorder. But feeling like you’re about to be ‘found out’ before delivering a big presentation, for example, is usually a sign that you’re being challenged or working outside your comfort zone, says Chamorro-Premuzic. “There is a very healthy degree somewhere that we’re not appreciating,” he adds (see ‘A toolkit for working with impostor syndrome’).

In scientists, impostor thoughts can simply be a by-product of thinking critically and approaching things with a healthy dose of scepticism, says Samantha Sutton, an independent career coach for scientists in Boston, Massachusetts. It’s also often a natural response to working in a high-achieving, competitive environment or towards an ambitious goal and should be normalized instead of treated as a problem to solve, she adds. “If you’re up against something massive, you should be scared,” says Sutton. When she communicates this to her clients, they are often relieved to hear that they don’t need to strive for total self-confidence before taking steps towards their goals. “They realize that nothing is wrong,” adds Sutton.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Bayern Munich are considering selling Jamal Musiala over concerns that his ongoing health problems will prevent him from returning to his best form.

Musiala, 23, was diagnosed with a “neurological dysfunction” after suffering an on-pitch collapse twice in a matter of days during pre-season friendlies against Heidenheim and RB Leipzig.

Industry observers note that the Germany international mentioned he was “very optimistic... there is no additional health risk beyond this” and indicated the condition would not hamper his highly promising career.

However, Bayern chief Karl-Heinz Rummenigge has now admitted that the club are assessing his future amid a downturn in performances, publicly questioning whether the club can now justify his lofty salary.

In a recent development, rummenigge told Sky Germany: “He has a health-related matter. It's also well known that he has a contract involving very substantial sums of money. As a club, we have to consider how to deal with that situation. I think that's responsible and perfectly normal.

“What we know unfortunately suggests it will be difficult for him to get back to the level he has often shown here in this stadium.”.

Musiala was reportedly Bayern’s best-paid player until Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane penned a contract extension earlier this month.

He has been limited to just four appearances in the Bundesliga this term due to a muscle injury, scoring one goal and notching one assist, with fitness problems continuing to plague him after spending over half of last season out with a broken leg.

Rummenigge states “a decision will have to be made” over his Musiala if he fails to show signs of improvement, but admitted that the former Chelsea academy product’s health complications would make a sale difficult.

Rummenigge added: “We need to talk to the family, the player, and the agency, because then these sums of money, sorry, with all due respect, are no longer feasible.

“I cannot imagine that Jamal wants to leave the club or that any other club would buy him under these conditions.

“We are all interested in his return, ideally in top form. But what happens if that isn’t the case? Then we still have to think about the finances.

“The discussion hasn’t taken place yet. These are just ideas at this stage.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By LEWIS BROWNING, SPORTS REPORTER.

Published: 12:23 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 20:01 EST, 22 November 2026.

Gary Neville led the criticism of Manchester United's defending in the opening minutes against Liverpool as Mauricio Pochettino's reign started in disastrous fashion at Anfield.

After just eight minutes, his aims were thrown into tatters when errors from Matthijs de Ligt and Leny Yoro saw the latter sent off before Liverpool took a swift lead.

A long ball from Ronald Araujo should have been dealt with easily by De Ligt, but the Dutchman found himself in no man's land, left the ball, and Alexander Isak raced clear.

That left Yoro scrambling to try to recover the situation for his side, but Isak stepped across him and he ended up fouling the Reds forward.

Referee Sam Barrott wasted no time in pulling out the red card, and United found themselves reduced to 10 men just minutes into a vital clash.

And former United defender Neville didn't hold back when it came to his analysis as he tore into the two players at fault.

In a recent development, leny Yoro is SENT OFF after eight minutes! 😱 pic.twitter.com/VKYvckvBBP.

Gary Neville torn into Manchester United duo Leny Yoro (right) and Matthijs de Ligt after the former was sent off.

Neville (pictured) questioned why the duo were playing as if they had 'never had basic training of how to play in defence'.

Industry observers note that 'When I saw De Ligt's name on the team sheet I have to admit I was absolutely stunned,' he stated, speaking on Sky Sports. 'And the reason I was stunned was because of this. If you'd watched him in Como four weeks ago he was very much well off it and that is just a basic ball over the top.

Recent findings suggest that 'It's his problem to start with, Yoro can be further across, but De Ligt is miles away from it, then Yoro has to get further round, he reacts late, his anticipation is poor. It's so clumsy from Yoro, he makes a lot of these types of mistakes.

'You could argue Isak delays to make sure Yoro runs into him, but it's naivety.'.

Pochettino was left scrambling to think of ideas to tighten up the defence but, before he could bring Harry Maguire on, it was 2-0 through Florian Wirtz.

Maguire eventually came on but it felt like too little, too late.

'We saw him in Como and he has been out for a year,' Neville continued on De Ligt. 'It is really tough to come back. To have him out there in a game like this, he has been exposed. Yoro's positioning is poor, he has to be across, you have to cover your mate. It is bad all around from United.

'Michael Carrick will be watching and say that's what I was having to deal with.'.

Sources indicate that and his criticism didn't stop there. After having the chance to re-watch the incident, Neville's criticism grew even stronger.

De Ligt (left) failed to deal with a long ball as Alexander Isak (right) raced away before the foul.

Former United captain Roy Keane (pictured) added that he was 'amazed' by the errors made.

It has been revealed that 'It's as bad defending from two centre backs defending a long ball as you will see,' the former defender, who likened a return from a year out to playing after six pints of alcohol, added. 'De Ligt is well out of it - he's been out so I have some sympathy. But between them, to let the ball beat you, it's unforgivable.

Sources indicate that 'It is shocking. Whilst Man United have those types of defenders in their team, they have no chance of keeping a clean sheet.

It has been revealed that 'It's basic understanding of how to play a position. It's the fundamentals. It's like these guys have never had basic training of how to play in defence.'.

Former United captain Roy Keane chimed in too, adding at half-time: 'It doesn't matter if it's a back four or back five, you do the basics right.

It has been revealed that 'I'm amazed at this level, I know he's been out a while, but it's really poor defending. He's never getting that ball.

'If you're a defender you always expect the worst. Isak's done well and I actually don't think he's going to get the ball.

According to recent reports, 'There's no way he's (Yoro) getting the ball, it's clumsy by United. Straight ball over the top and he's in major trouble. But there's no way he's getting that ball. I know he's quick and sharp but it's really poor defending. Players not smelling danger.'.

Industry News: COP31 draft deal calls for 'immediate' shift away from fossil fuels

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1005 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • COP31 co-host Australia has kicked off the second week of climate talks in Antalya with a draft political deal calling for an "immediate transition away from fossil fuels" and a "tripling" of finance for climate adaptation measures in developing countries to at least $120 billion (€109 billion).
  • In a recent development, the goal of other co-host Turkey to increase electrification of the world's economies to 35% by 2035 also features in the text.
  • Language around a faster phaseout of oil, coal and gas is key because fossil-fuel producing nations have repeatedly pushed back against stronger wording in previous COP decisions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

COP31 co-host Australia has kicked off the second week of climate talks in Antalya with a draft political deal calling for an "immediate transition away from fossil fuels" and a "tripling" of finance for climate adaptation measures in developing countries to at least $120 billion (€109 billion).

In a recent development, the goal of other co-host Turkey to increase electrification of the world's economies to 35% by 2035 also features in the text. The draft emphasizes clean energy but notes that "electrification can provide co-benefits regardless of the electricity mix" — an approach that has proved divisive at the talks, with many insisting that electrification be strictly tied to renewable energy.

Language around a faster phaseout of oil, coal and gas is key because fossil-fuel producing nations have repeatedly pushed back against stronger wording in previous COP decisions.

"The fresh negotiating text contains all the necessary building blocks for a successful outcome to the conference: from the goal of climate neutrality for all industrialized countries by 2030 to a work program that can keep the 1.5-degree limit in place," mentioned Greenpeace Germany head Martin Kaiser on Monday.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The draft expressed "deep concern" that the 1.5 Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) temperature threshold agreed at the 2015 COP in Paris to avoid runaway climate change was now out of reach. It stressed the need for "accelerating action to minimize both the magnitude and duration of any temperature overshoot and to return global warming to below 1.5C as soon as possible.".

Recognizing a need to address rising carbon emissions, the draft highlighted efforts to "urgently and rapidly" scale up controversial technologies to capture and store CO2 to bring down atmospheric carbon levels.

According to recent reports, "For the first time, all the parties here are grappling with the fact that the world will inevitably exceed 1.5 degrees. Negotiators must deliver a response," said Ani Dasgupta, president of the World Resources Institute, adding that this meant going beyond slashing emissions.

"This requires scaling carbon removal through both nature-based solutions like restoring forests and wetlands, or emerging technologies that directly capture carbon from air," he told reporters.

Kaiser, however, criticized the lack of binding commitments in the draft's resolutions. He added that Europe should work with China and the most climate-vulnerable countries to keep oil-producing nations, including Russia and countries in the Middle East, from "undermining the conference's decisions and turning them into a free pass for the oil and gas industry.".

Other activists have dismissed carbon capture as a "false solution" being promoted by corporations.

Cosima Cassel, an expert at climate think tank E3G, was cautiously pleased with the draft's "ambitious language" but noted it appeared the broad deal would now leave negotiators to "fight for trade-offs.".

"The test will be whether the final decision keeps the core elements once that process plays out: ambition on overshoot, defense of the science, clean electrification and forward progress on adaptation finance," she said in a statement.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Disagreements over financing largely relate to who should bear the costs of international climate action, whether financial support should be provided through grants or loans, and how funding for developing countries can be increased.

Representatives of developing nations and small island states, regions bearing the brunt of the climate crisis, have protested climate inaction and a lack of financial support in recent days.

"Climate finance isn't an extra at these talks: it's the condition for everything else," said Rukiya Khamis, program manager for East Africa with environmental group 350.org. "It's alarming how financial pledges by wealthy, polluting countries are dropping like a stone — COP31 must stop this with a strong outcome on adaptation finance.".

"Now we must fight to keep this [adaption finance] in the final decision and ensure these promises become real, grant-based money," noted Harjeet Singh of the Fill The Fund campaign, which calls on rich countries and corporations to deliver the funding needed for climate-related loss and damage, such as homes destroyed by floods and harvests ruined by drought.

"Communities are suffering devastating losses and damages today precisely because we failed to deliver adaptation at the right time," added Singh.

At 18 pages and 144 items, the draft will be the focus of lengthy discussions in the coming days as delegates try to come to an agreement by Friday. Some observers went so far as to say the document's scope was too wide to be taken seriously.

"The draft final declaration reads like a Christmas wish list," stated Niklas Höhne, a climate policy expert at the NewClimate Institute in Germany. "There are even several points on which we will obviously not be able to reach a consensus, including for example the proposal that developed countries achieve net-zero emissions by 2030.".

But Chris Bowen, chief of negotiations and Australia's minister for climate change and energy, appeared optimistic.

Sources indicate that "The general tenor and tone [of the talks] has been very constructive," he told reporters Monday. "Parties have come to me with strong views about various things, as you'd expect […] [but] they've also come in the spirit of cooperation, the spirit of respect and a spirit where parties have mentioned to me that they want to help get an outcome.".

David Waskow, director of WRI's International Climate Initiative, remarked the draft text highlighted a level of "seriousness" on vital concerns like finance, electrification, oceans, overshoot scenarios and emissions of greenhouse gases including methane, which has a warming impact more than 80 times stronger than CO2.

"The question is whether the level of ambition on those complications is carried through into the final outcome here," noted Waskow. "And that's what we need to be watching closely over the coming days.".

Additional reporting by Tim Schauenberg in Antalya.

Enhancement, November 17, 2026: This article has been updated with additional reactions to the draft text.

Which Premier League players are set for yellow card suspensions?

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Harry Maguire and Alexis Mac Allister are among 13 players on the brink of a one-match ban.
  • The first one-match suspensions for yellow card offences in the 2026-27 Premier League season have now been served.
  • Hull City's Matt Crooks and Aston Villa's Matty Cash became the first players to receive a ban for accumulating five yellow cards before gameweek 19.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Harry Maguire and Alexis Mac Allister are among 13 players on the brink of a one-match ban.

The first one-match suspensions for yellow card offences in the 2026-27 Premier League season have now been served.

Hull City's Matt Crooks and Aston Villa's Matty Cash became the first players to receive a ban for accumulating five yellow cards before gameweek 19.

Players receive a one-match suspension if they pick up five or more yellow cards prior to the conclusion of their team's 19th league match of the season.

There are now 13 players sitting on four bookings after 10 rounds of matches, meaning they must avoid another yellow card prior to the halfway point of the season to avoid a ban.

Bournemouth have the most players on the brink of a ban, with three players one yellow card away from suspension.

After that date, the threshold increases to 10 yellow cards. Any player reaching that number before the end of their club's 32nd league match of the season will receive a two-match suspension.

From that point, there are further thresholds at 15 and 20 yellow cards.

According to recent reports, for players reaching 15 cautions, they incur a three-match suspension. Punishments for players reaching 20 yellow cards are determined by a regulatory commission.

Those cut-offs do not reset until the end of the Premier League season.

In the Championship, League One and League Two, there are similar thresholds.

However, with those three divisions having 46 rounds of league matches instead of 38, players have to avoid getting 10 yellow cards before the end of the 37th league match in order to not receive a two-match suspension.

In those divisions, the yellow cards are reset at the end of the league season and do not include matches in the play-offs.

The following players have served a one-match ban and will now receive a two-match ban if they reach ten bookings before game week 32:.

Matt Crooks - Hull City (five yellow cards).

Matty Cash - Aston Villa (five).

If any of the following players receive another Premier League yellow card before the season's halfway point, they will be banned for one match:.

Vitaly Janelt - Brentford (four).

Oli McBurnie - Hull City (four).

Harry Maguire - Manchester United (four).

Pascal Gross - Brighton & Hove Albion (four).

Ethan Ampadu - Leeds United (four).

Oliver Boscagli - Brighton & Hove Albion (four).

Adam Smith - Bournemouth (four).

Marcus Tavernier - Bournemouth (four).

Antonio Silve - Bournemouth (four).

Yeremy Pino - Crystal Palace (four).

Alexis Mac Allister - Liverpool (four).

James McAtee - Nottingham Forest (four).

The following players will miss their club's next set of fixtures:.

Max Dowman - Arsenal (red card suspension).

Jean-Philippe Mateta - Crystal Palace (red card suspension).

Igor Thiago - Brentford (red card suspension).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An 18-year-old who has played at two major international tournaments and the division’s top clearance maker from last season also feature.

A tricky, exciting, quick and versatile midfielder, Azeez has proven himself in the Championship with Millwall over the past two seasons and now deserves a chance to test himself in the top flight.

Recent findings suggest that brighton had been chasing him for a while and struck a deal on deadline day for a very reasonable reported initial £12.5m, rising to £15m. If he can make the step up and produce anything like his second-tier form, he’ll be a steal.

It has been revealed that he is a high-volume producer at the sharp end of the pitch, constantly making things happen that threaten the opposition’s goal, but standing out most for his crossing. He ranked top of the Championship last season for open-play crosses (227) and expected assists from crosses (6.71 xA).

He also ranked fourth for dribble attempts (131), ninth for shots (95), sixth for chances created from open play (58). He created good-quality chances, too; only two players created more substantial chances than he did (18), and he ranked fourth for expected assists. His 9.12 xA alongside only seven assists suggests he may benefit from playing alongside better finishers.

A hugely exciting prospect. Despite being 18, Mbaye has significant and noteworthy experience under his belt. Last year he made six appearances, including in the final, for Senegal at the Africa Cup of Nations and this summer he made four appearances at the World Cup. He has also played in two Ligue 1 title-winning campaigns, including 2024-25, when he became the youngest player in PSG’s history to start a game, and won the Champions League in both of those seasons.

He is a dribbling and ball-carrying menace, who always looks as if he’s about to do something special. Among players to play at least 900 minutes in Ligue 1 last season, he was 11th for carries (moving at least five metres with the ball) per 90, with 20.0, and 12th for progressive carries (moving at least five metres upfield with the ball) per 90, with 10.3. Most of the players above him in both lists are defenders, who naturally have more space to move into.

Recent findings suggest that he was third for take-on-ending carries, or running with the ball for at least five metres before attempting to beat an opponent with a dribble, with 2.9 per 90. And he also has end product to boot. He scored at Afcon and the World Cup despite limited minutes and his 0.45 goals or assists per 90 for PSG last season is not to be sniffed at.

Danso had a pretty impossible task over his two years at Tottenham. He was the back-up to the first-choice centre-backs Cristian Romero and Micky van de Ven, playing intermittently on both sides of central defence in dysfunctional teams jumping between styles of play, and he very rarely played for any consistent run of games.

He was unfairly compared with the players he was replacing for much of his time there, but the truth is he was always reliable enough. He excelled, however, when Romero got injured during the run-in last season and he was called upon in Spurs’ time of need as they scraped clear of relegation.

He may not be the best on the ball – though he is hardly terrible – but he is an excellent deep defender. Among those to play at least 1,000 minutes in the Premier League last season, Danso ranked first for clearances (8.2 per 90) and headed clearances (6.3), and was fifth for aerial duels won (4.8 per 90).

He could thrive at Sunderland, who spent more of their out-of-possession game time in a low block than any other team in the Premier League last season (25%). Danso could be perfectly at home in this setup, paired alongside the player he beat into second place for clearances and headed clearances: Dan Ballard.

It was always said during Pep Guardiola’s time at Manchester City that attackers had their wings clipped in terms of individual freedom, limited to playing within the parameters of the manager’s meticulous gameplan.

But dribbling ability became increasingly crucial in the final years of his reign, with Jérémy Doku and Antoine Semenyo on the wings and Rayan Cherki in between. Doku (162) and Semenyo (144) ranked first and second for dribbles attempted in the Premier League last season, with Cherki ninth (111). They also ranked first (84), fourth (59) and eighth (51), respectively, for dribbles completed.

Industry observers note that with the deadline-day addition of Ndiaye, City have gone in even harder on dribbling ability under Enzo Maresca. The Senegal international ranked second for dribbles attempted (136) and dribbles completed (73) in the Premier League last season.

Fernandez-Pardo’s versatility is a major attraction. He’s comfortable playing off the left and cutting in on to his right foot, or as a No 9. Although not the bulkiest, he has explosive pace and promises to be a threat in behind.

The Belgium international is arguably at his most threatening when running with the ball because he does so with such purpose. His 122 carries progressing the ball at least 10 metres upfield in Ligue 1 last term were bettered by only seven players, several of whom were defenders.

On top of that, he ranked top for carries into the penalty area (69) and seventh for carries ending with a shot or chance created (39).

Industry observers note that fofana appeared to be enjoying a swift rise in 2024-25, only for a serious ankle injury to massively disrupt his development in 2025-26. Sunderland will be hoping they can get him back to the levels shown the season before last, when he was a real livewire on Lyon’s left flank.

Recent findings suggest that he contributed nine goal involvements (five goals, four assists) in 1,586 minutes in Ligue 1 in 2024-25, averaging one every 176 minutes. Only eight forwards (900+ mins) averaged more expected assists per 90 (0.25).

The most eye-catching aspects of his game, however, were his dynamism and pace. He could be difficult to stop once moving, and this made him a very useful outlet. Among Ligue 1 forwards (900+ mins), his 16.6 carries per 90 ranked him sixth, and he moved up to third for progressive carries per 90 (11.5).

In a recent development, fofana is direct, exciting and has significant potential. He is a player Sunderland could make a profit on if he reaches the levels previously expected.

Andrés arrived to bolster Brighton’s midfield options after Carlos Baleba’s exit to Manchester United. Although a different type of midfielder to the Cameroonian, Chema is another with vast potential.

A product of Real Madrid’s academy, Chema joined Stuttgart last summer. During his sole campaign in the Bundesliga, he was in and out of the team but caught the eye at the base of their midfield.

It has been revealed that comparisons have been made to Rodri because of his physical attributes and nominal role as a holding midfielder. He doesn’t have anything like the same influence in possession but Chema is tidy on the ball.

It’s what he offers defensively that is most notable, however. He’s been broadly praised for his anticipation and reading of the game, ranking second among midfielders (900+ mins) since the start of last season for interceptions per 90 in the Bundesliga (2.3).

Thomas Tuchel may not have planned it this way, but in one night he gave us all the rich history of the England team at once: some glorious attacking football, some self-sabotage defending, a red card, a late siege and a fight.

Industry observers note that this was the beguiling story of Spain 2 England 3, an evening that began with the world champions parading the World Cup trophy and ended with 10 Englishmen defending a lead with their last breath. England beat the world champions in Madrid, and for more than 30 minutes including injury time they did so with 10 men, Dan Burn heading the last ball out as per the tradition of a defensive rearguard action.

In a recent development, this was the game that had it all: including a substitute, in Djed Spence, who had already picked up a yellow card on the bench before he came on. It was a coming-of-age performance in goal for James Trafford. It has been revealed that this is the first time England have faced Spain in Madrid since November 2004 when they were beaten 1-0 in the Santiago Bernabéu, a game that was ravaged by obscene chanting. The nations were supposed to play a fixture in the Spanish capital in 2008, but the Football Association insisted it be moved to Seville instead.

Earlier this year, Spanish supporters brought shame on themselves again after a flurry of anti-Muslim chants marred a friendly against Egypt; they were fined $20,000 by Fifa and must play their next friendly in a partially closed stadium.

There will be a full house in the Wanda Metropolitano on Sunday night, as the reigning world and European champions aim to defend their extraordinary unbeaten run of 43 games, and England head coach Tuchel is adamant the atmosphere will be in keeping with the occasion.

The German has, however, made it clear he and his staff will use their platform before the contest to remind England’s players of the steps they should take if the worst scenario unfolds.

According to recent reports, asked about incidents that had pockmarked this fixture before, Tuchel remarked: “I think I hear it the first time that this happens. I think it’s unacceptable. In any stadium, not even in stadiums, we will never accept racism. We will never be racist towards anyone.

England are a seeded side for the Nations League quarter-finals after topping their group.

The draw for the final eight teams in the 2026-27 Nations League will be on Friday, 20 November at 11:00 GMT.

It will take place at Uefa's headquarters in Nyon, Switzerland and be broadcast on Uefa TV.

England are the only home nation to have made it to the quarter-final stage, however Northern Ireland's draw against Hungary saw them top Group B2 and secure promotion to League A in the 2028-29 tournament.

Scotland will remain in League B following their third-place finish in Group B1, and Wales face a League A/B relegation play-off in March after being consigned to last place in Group A4.

The Republic of Ireland finished second in Group B3 and so will take part in a League A/B promotion play-off in March.

The winners of groups A1-A4 are seeded for the draw, playing the runners-up of other groups in League A.

England have sealed their place in the last eight as Group A3 winners and could face:.

They cannot face A3 runners-up Spain as teams must be drawn against sides from other groups.

The quarter-finals will be played over two legs during the international break between 25-30 March.

Seeded teams get to play the second leg of their quarter-final at home.

Nations that reach the semi-finals can bid those penultimate matches as well as the final.

The remaining dates for the Nations League are:.

Quarter-finals first leg: 25-27 March.

Quarter-finals second leg: 28-30 March.

Semi-finals, third-place play-off and final: 9-13 June.

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Wild scenes erupted at the MKM Stadium as Oli McBurnie scored a stoppage-time double to snatch a late victory for Hull over title challengers Brighton.

The Tigers had not won since they beat Coventry in late August, drawing five times since, but they withstood a barrage of attacks - with home goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis producing an immediate display - and stole a 2-0 win against the run of play.

The MKM Stadium has become something of a fortress and Brighton had never enjoyed success on Humberside.

But the Seagulls have been in immense form, with many talking of a serious title tilt, and arrived in Hull second in the table and with the chance to close to within three points of leaders Arsenal.

Fabian Hurzeler’s side were dominant but could not find a way through, thwarted on several occasions by Tzolakis, and failed to distance themselves from third-placed Manchester City, who dropped points at home to Fulham on Saturday.

Brighton push for an eighth victory of the season was halted by Joao Costinha’s dismissal a minute from time for a second yellow card and, from there, the wheels came off.

McBurnie bundled home a fine Hull move two minutes into stoppage time and the Tigers were not done there as the striker buried his fourth goal in as many matches to lift his side up to 11th in the table.

A quarter of an hour in Tzolakis was forced into a deft save as Diego Gomez picked up a dangerous Maxim De Cuyper cross and nearly made in 1-0, with the keeper blocking a shot from Georginio Rutter with his legs on the half-hour.

As the first half drew to a close, Yasin Ayari hit the bar and Rutter got to the rebound, but Tzolakis produced another impressive save to ensure all was level going into the break – with a late Brighton penalty shout dismissed as Pascal Gross felt he had been pushed in the goalmouth.

Hull went close to breaking the deadlock after 64 minutes when Mohamed Belloumi darted through Brighton’s defence but fired what was a valuable chance wide.

Just over 10 minutes later Tigers’ hopes were raised again as substitute Sorba Thomas breathed fresh life into the game by hitting the woodwork, after which Hull looked dangerous again when Thomas pushed forward but was foiled by Dunk.

Costinha was shown a second yellow card for pushing Thomas and it was the break Hull needed. Regan Slater played in Lucas Gourna-Douath, who picked out McBurnie to prod into the bottom corner.

Before the dust had settled, the Tigers were on the move again with McBurnie the man at the forefront once more as he linked up with Belloumi to find space in front of an open goal in the 95th minute to seal the win.

#70985. The AfD and neo-Nazi networks: How close are the connections?

The AfD and neo-Nazi networks: How close are the connections?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1164 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The electoral successes of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) have brought the party closer than ever to taking power in Germany.
  • This raises an even sharper question: what political ideas does the party stand for, which has been classified by Germany's domestic intelligence agency as a "suspected right-wing extremist" organization and, in several federal states, is already considered "confirmed right-wing extremist"?
  • Many political scientists have observed that the AfD has become increasingly radicalized since its founding in 2013.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The electoral successes of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) have brought the party closer than ever to taking power in Germany. For the 2029 federal election, it has set itself an ambitious goal: to see its co-chair Alice Weidel to become Germany's next chancellor.

This raises an even sharper question: what political ideas does the party stand for, which has been classified by Germany's domestic intelligence agency as a "suspected right-wing extremist" organization and, in several federal states, is already considered "confirmed right-wing extremist"?

Many political scientists have observed that the AfD has become increasingly radicalized since its founding in 2013.

"Viewed as a whole, the AfD is an extreme right-wing party that also displays tendencies associated with a fascist movement," said Fabian Virchow, a researcher on right-wing extremism at Düsseldorf University of Applied Sciences, in an interview with DW.

In a recent development, virchow identifies different factions and strategic tendencies within the party, some of which are at odds with one another. Party leader Alice Weidel, for example, is generally seen as a proponent of a free-market approach that seeks to keep the state as small as possible. Others, by contrast, favor a strong state shaped by an ethnically homogeneous people, among them Björn Höcke, the influential far-right AfD leader in the state of Thuringia.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Virchow sees a "normalization" of right-wing extremist positions within the AfD. In his view, this has made the party more attractive to neo-Nazi circles: "Today, many people see greater room for ethnonationalist and radical right-wing ideas.".

Support for this observation comes from the latest findings of the Leipzig Authoritarianism Study, one of the most widely cited long-term studies tracking right-wing extremist attitudes in Germany. The researchers behind the study have identified a rise in right-wing extremist views within German society, including a growing acceptance of ideologies rooted in the tradition of National Socialism.

In a recent development, particularly striking is the finding that around two-thirds of people with firmly entrenched far-right worldviews would vote for the AfD. According to the study, the AfD has achieved what earlier far-right parties in Germany never managed: "to unite large segments of the electorate with anti-democratic attitudes behind it.".

According to recent reports, the debate has been further fueled by several recent incidents within the party. In 2026 alone, numerous AfD politicians and staff members made headlines over alleged ties to neo-Nazi organizations:.

In August 2026, police carried out a large-scale raid targeting fifteen people. Authorities suspect them of continuing the activities of the so-called "Artgemeinschaft." Before it was banned in 2023, the group was considered one of Germany's largest and most influential neo-Nazi cadre organizations. Particularly explosive was the fact that two of those targeted in the raid are sitting AfD members of the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament. Their attorneys deny the allegations.

According to reporting by the German daily, Welt, four staff members of the AfD's parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt are former members of the now-banned "Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend" (HDJ), a neo-Nazi youth organization rooted in National Socialist racial ideology that organized paramilitary camps for young people. Two of the staff members held leadership positions within the HDJ and now work closely with AfD politician Ulrich Siegmund, who is seeking to become the AfD's first state premier in December.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Sources indicate that remarkably, both organizations, the "Artgemeinschaft" and the HDJ, are on the AfD's so-called incompatibility list, which is intended to draw a line between the party and extremist organizations and movements. In principle, anyone with a history of membership in such groups is supposed to be excluded from the party.

But the list appears to be little more than a dead letter. In 2020, former AfD federal executive board member Andreas Kalbitz was expelled from the party after failing to disclose his membership in the "Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend" on his application to join. Yet according to the news magazine Spiegel, he is once again working for the AfD, this time as a staffer for Saxony-Anhalt state legislator Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, who has since become deputy speaker of the state parliament.

It has been revealed that the question of the AfD's relationship to National Socialism has dogged the party since its founding in 2013. Even in its early years, co-founder and first party leader Bernd Lucke sparked controversy when he described democracy and parliamentary politics in Germany as "degenerate," a term the Nazis used to disparage art and culture that did not conform to their ideological worldview.

In Germany, references to the Nazi dictatorship (1933-1945) under Adolf Hitler remain politically taboo because of the country's responsibility for World War Two and the Holocaust, the systematic mass murder of Europe's Jews.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

If AfD members or their staff have come under scrutiny because of past involvement in ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations, they have generally sought to distance themselves from those backgrounds or from the ideologies associated with them.

But how credible are these attempts at distancing? Laura Neumann* has worked with many people seeking to leave the far-right scene. She works for "Nordverbund Ausstieg Rechts," a network of organizations that supports far-right cadres and activists as they disengage from the movement. "A successful exit is the result of a professionally guided process," she stated in an interview with DW.

Neumann describes leaving the far-right scene as a challenging process of self-confrontation. "When it comes to someone leaving the movement, the first question I always ask is: How does that person talk about their past? Have they genuinely come to terms with it?".

Based on the experience of exit counselors, one principle generally holds true: the longer and more deeply a person has been immersed in far-right circles, the more difficult it becomes to distance themselves from those beliefs and affiliations.

Sources indicate that DW requested a statement from the AfD's federal executive board regarding its handling of party members who were previously active in ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations. Individual lawmakers and parliamentary staff members were also asked to comment. None responded.

The party's and its politicians' silence in the face of such allegations reflects an observation made by political scientist Fabian Virchow: "Within the AfD, there is no longer a perceived need to distance oneself from radical far-right positions. That is part of this process of normalization.".

Virchow says that right-wing extremism appears to have advanced so far into the mainstream of German society that efforts to scandalize it now remain largely ineffective.
